planting.note: Plant corms immediately after division in late summer or early fall, 3-4 inches deep, in well-drained, calcareous prairie or glade soil in partial shade to full sun; unlike its woodland relatives, prairie trout lily is native to open tallgrass prairie and limestone glades from Texas to Kansas and Missouri and tolerates more sun and drier summer soil.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep immediately after division in late summer or early fall in well-drained, calcareous prairie or rocky glade soil in partial shade to full sun. Prairie trout lily is a Great Plains counterpart to the woodland Erythronium species, native to tallgrass prairie remnants and limestone glades from central Texas north through Kansas and Missouri, where its plain green, unmottled to faintly mottled leaves and pale lavender-white, star-shaped flowers appear in very early spring and are held more upright than the nodding blooms of its forest cousins. Because it grows naturally in open, sun-exposed prairie rather than deep shade, it tolerates a drier, better-drained garden spot than most trout lilies, making it a good fit for a native prairie or rock-garden planting rather than a woodland border. Like other trout lilies it goes fully dormant by late spring, so mark the spot and interplant with warm-season prairie grasses or forbs that fill in as it disappears.

planting.note: Plant corms immediately after division in late summer or early fall, 3-4 inches deep, in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; dimpled trout lily is the common southeastern trout lily of rich cove forests and floodplain woods from Georgia and the Carolinas into Alabama and Tennessee.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep immediately after division in late summer or early fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil under deciduous trees; do not allow corms to dry out before planting. Dimpled trout lily takes its name from the distinctly dimpled, umbilicate seed capsule that lies flat on the ground as it ripens, a reliable field mark separating it from the similar Erythronium americanum, which holds its capsule upright on an erect stalk; both share the same mottled, trout-spotted leaves and nodding, reflexed yellow flowers in late winter to early spring. It forms dense, slowly spreading colonies in rich southeastern cove forests and floodplain woods and makes an excellent naturalizing companion for trilliums, bloodroot, and other regional spring ephemerals. Like other trout lilies it disappears completely by late spring, so plant it where later-emerging ferns or hostas can take over the display.

planting.note: Plant corms immediately after division in late summer or early fall, 3-4 inches deep, in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Henderson's fawn lily is native to open oak woodlands and rocky slopes of southwest Oregon and northern California and, unlike many Erythronium, wants sharper drainage and a summer-dry dormant period.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep immediately after division in late summer or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; give it a spot that dries out in summer, mimicking the Mediterranean-climate oak woodlands of southwest Oregon and northern California where it grows wild. Henderson's fawn lily is among the showiest western trout lilies, with heavily mottled leaves and one to several nodding, lilac to soft purple flowers marked with a dark maroon zone at the throat, blooming in March and April on slopes that are damp in winter and spring but bone-dry by early summer. Because it is adapted to that wet-winter, dry-summer rhythm rather than the consistently moist soil eastern woodland species prefer, it performs best in a rock garden, raised bed, or bulb frame with excellent drainage where summer irrigation can be withheld once the foliage yellows. Source corms only from nurseries propagating responsibly, since wild populations are localized and slow to recover from collection.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in fall in deep, moist, rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade in a cove-forest woodland setting; sweet wakerobin grows in the same rich southern Appalachian coves as the closely related Trillium vaseyi and Trillium erectum.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in fall in deep, moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade. Sweet wakerobin is a southern Appalachian pedicellate trillium, native to rich cove forests of North Carolina, Tennessee, and Georgia, easily confused in the field with its relatives Trillium vaseyi and Trillium erectum but distinguished by its pure white, outward-facing petals held above the leaves and a light, sweet fragrance rather than the fetid odor typical of many large trilliums. It blooms in April and May, later than most sessile trilliums, and slowly forms an expanding clump where the deep, consistently moist cove-forest conditions it needs are maintained. Give it the richest, most humus-laden soil available and a thick annual leaf-litter mulch, and expect several years before divisions reach full flowering size, since trillium rhizomes resent disturbance and recover slowly from transplant.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (Weakley)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart in fall, 6-10 weeks before first frost, in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; prairie camas is native to tallgrass prairies and rocky glades of the southern Great Plains and Ozarks and blooms later than most Camassia species.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade in fall for a late-spring bloom. Prairie camas is native to tallgrass prairie remnants, rocky glades, and open woodland edges from Missouri and Kansas south into Oklahoma, Arkansas, and Texas, where its tall spikes of pale blue-violet, star-shaped flowers open several weeks later than those of the more commonly grown Camassia scilloides and quamash, extending the native-bulb bloom season into early summer. Like other camassias it tolerates the heavier clay soils common on the southern plains and naturalizes readily in a sunny meadow or prairie planting, where its dying foliage can be masked by warm-season grasses filling in around it. Leave clumps undisturbed to bulk up for several years before dividing, and let the foliage yellow and wither fully before removing it so the bulb can store energy for next year's bloom.

planting.note: Sprinkle seed on the surface of moist, acidic, nutrient-poor medium (milled sphagnum or 50/50 peat and sand) without covering; keep standing in a tray of pure rain water or distilled water in full sun to partial shade — small butterwort is the tiniest of the Gulf Coast Pinguicula species and grows naturally in open, wet pine savanna.

directions: Small butterwort is the smallest of the native Gulf Coast Pinguicula, forming a flat rosette barely an inch or two across of pale yellow-green, sticky-glandular leaves that trap and digest tiny insects such as gnats and fungus flies, growing naturally in the open, wet, acidic pine savannas and seepage bogs of the Gulf and Atlantic coastal plains. Delicate pale lavender to white flowers, each on a thin, wiry stalk well above the foliage, appear from spring into summer and self-seed readily in suitably wet, nutrient-poor conditions. Sow seed on the surface of milled sphagnum or a lean peat-sand mix and keep the pot standing in pure rain water or distilled water year-round in full sun to light shade, since tap water minerals and ordinary fertile soil will kill it within a season. It is easiest to grow alongside sundews and smaller Sarracenia species in a shallow, sunny bog garden or a bog-in-a-pot on a porch.
sources: Carnivorous Plants of the Southeast (Larry Mellichamp)

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated bulbs or scales in fall, 4-6 inches deep, in consistently moist to wet, acidic, sandy-peaty soil in full sun to partial shade; sandhills bog lily is native to fire-maintained seepage bogs and streamhead pocosins of the North Carolina and Virginia Sandhills and needs steady moisture year-round.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated bulbs or scales 4-6 inches deep in fall in consistently moist to wet, acidic, sandy-peaty soil in full sun to partial shade. Sandhills bog lily is a rare, narrowly distributed native lily discovered growing in the fire-maintained longleaf pine seepage bogs and streamhead pocosins of the North Carolina and Virginia Sandhills, where recurring fire keeps competing shrubs low and lets its tall, wiry stems and nodding, orange-red, strongly recurved Turk's-cap-type flowers stand out in mid to late summer. Unlike most garden lilies it wants year-round wet feet rather than the well-drained soil most Lilium demand, making it best suited to the sunny, boggy margin of a rain garden or pond edge alongside pitcher plants and sundews rather than a conventional lily border. Because natural populations are small and highly restricted, plant only nursery-propagated bulbs, and mulch lightly with pine straw to hold moisture and suppress weeds around the shallow root system.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (Weakley)
